title: Hash maps: how they work, and when they degrade
story:
Finding a record among many normally means searching: examining entries until the right one appears, or narrowing the range by comparisons. Either way the cost grows with the number of records.

Hans Peter Luhn, at IBM, is credited with the first description of hashing with chaining, in an internal memorandum of January 1953. The idea removes the search entirely: pass the key through a function producing an index, and address an array position directly rather than looking for the key.

That is worth pausing on, because the step is easy to take for granted. The lookup does not get faster; it stops being a lookup. The location is computed from the thing being looked up, so nothing is examined and rejected along the way. That is why the cost does not depend on how many entries exist — the work is the same whether the table holds ten items or ten million.

Two different keys can of course produce the same index, and the structure must cope. Either entries sharing a position are kept together in a list at that position, or a deterministic rule finds another free position. Either way the operation now involves examining the entries that share the position, which is fine as long as the number sharing it stays small.

That last clause is the whole of the caveat, and it deserves stating precisely because the constant-time claim is usually quoted without it. Constant time is an expectation, not a guarantee, and the expectation rests on the keys being spread across the array. If they are not, everything lands in the same position, the structure degenerates into a single list, and the operation is linear in the number of entries there. The good case and the bad case have the same code and the same appearance.

Which sets up the part worth knowing, because it turns a theoretical caveat into a vulnerability. An attacker who knows or can determine the hash function may submit keys chosen to collide, concentrating them in one position deliberately. This was demonstrated against many widely deployed web platforms in 2011, allowing a small request to consume disproportionate processing time. The submitted data was small and well-formed, the server accepted it as ordinary input, and the cost of processing it was enormous.

Note the shape of that attack, because it generalises beyond hash tables. It exploits a gap between the average case, which is what the system was designed and measured against, and the worst case, which is reachable by anyone who can choose the inputs. Any structure whose performance depends on its input being typical has the same exposure, and the assumption of typical input is usually invisible in the code.

The standard mitigation is to introduce a per-process random seed into the hash, so that an attacker cannot predict which keys collide. Note what it does and does not achieve: it does not improve the worst case, which remains linear. It makes the worst case unreachable on purpose, which is a different kind of protection — a defence against a chosen input rather than against an unlucky one.

The other costs are worth stating since the structure is often treated as free. It trades memory for speed and must keep spare capacity, because a table filled close to its size collides constantly; so it is resized as it fills, and that resize rehashes every entry, meaning an individual insertion can occasionally be far more expensive than the average suggests. And iteration order is a consequence of the hash function rather than of insertion, so any code that relies on the order is relying on something that was never promised.

problem.name: Computed location
problem.shape: Entries must be found by key, repeatedly, among many.
tell: lookup cost is assumed constant with no statement about the keys
keys come from outside the system
a latency spike coincides with an insertion rather than a lookup
code depends on the order entries come back in
problem.move: Use the expectation deliberately: it holds while keys spread across the array, so ask where the keys come from. Where they can be chosen by someone else, seed the hash per process so the worst case cannot be reached on purpose, and treat iteration order as unspecified.
problem.invariant: The location is computed from the key rather than searched for, so the cost does not depend on how many entries exist — provided the keys spread. Where they do not, the structure degenerates into a list and the operation is linear.
problem.breaks: Constant time is an expectation resting on an assumption about the keys, and that assumption is invisible in the code. An adversary who can choose keys can violate it deliberately, so a structure measured as fast on typical input can be made arbitrarily slow by anyone supplying the input.

cost.time: resizing rehashes every entry, so an occasional insertion is far more expensive than the average implies
cost.space: spare capacity must be kept, because a table filled close to its size collides constantly
cost.beats: a sorted structure, which guarantees logarithmic time rather than expecting constant time and keeps order, and a plain list, which needs no assumptions about keys and searches everything

worked.problem: What makes a hash table degrade, and why can the degradation be triggered deliberately?
worked.reasoning:
It degrades when the keys stop spreading across the array, and that can be triggered deliberately because the spreading is an assumption about the input rather than a property of the structure.

Start with what the structure does, since the failure follows from it. Rather than searching, the location is computed from the key: pass the key through a function producing an index, and address that array position directly. The lookup does not get faster — it stops being a lookup, because nothing is examined and rejected along the way. That is why the cost does not depend on how many entries exist.

Two keys can produce the same index, so the structure copes by keeping colliding entries together at a position or by finding another free position by a deterministic rule. Either way the operation now involves examining the entries sharing that position, which is fine while the number sharing it stays small.

That clause is the whole caveat. Constant time is an expectation, not a guarantee, and the expectation rests on keys being spread. If they all land in the same position the structure degenerates into a single list and the operation is linear in the number of entries there. The good case and the bad case have identical code and appearance.

Which makes the deliberate version straightforward: an attacker who knows or can determine the hash function submits keys chosen to collide, concentrating them in one position. This was demonstrated against many widely deployed web platforms in 2011, letting a small request consume disproportionate processing time — the data was small, well-formed and accepted as ordinary input, and processing it was enormously expensive.

The shape of that attack is the transferable part, and I would say it explicitly: it exploits the gap between the average case, which is what the system was designed and measured against, and the worst case, which is reachable by anyone who can choose the inputs. Any structure whose performance depends on its input being typical has the same exposure, and the assumption of typical input is usually invisible in the code.

The mitigation is a per-process random seed in the hash, so an attacker cannot predict which keys collide. What it does and does not do is worth being precise about: it does not improve the worst case, which is still linear. It makes the worst case unreachable on purpose — a defence against a chosen input rather than an unlucky one.

Two further costs, since the structure gets treated as free. It must keep spare capacity, because a table filled close to its size collides constantly, so it resizes as it fills — and a resize rehashes every entry, meaning an occasional insertion is far more expensive than the average suggests, which shows up as a latency spike on a write rather than a read. And iteration order follows from the hash function rather than from insertion, so code depending on the order is depending on something never promised.

problem.practice: Find a hash map in your system whose keys come from user input and check whether the language seeds its hash per process. Then look for anything iterating a map and depending on the order it comes back in.

beats.broke: Finding a record among many required searching, so the cost of a lookup grew with the number of records however they were arranged.
beats.fix: Compute the location from the key itself, so the operation addresses a position directly and stops being a search at all — which is why cost stops depending on how many entries exist.
beats.cost: The constant time is an expectation resting on an assumption about the keys, and an adversary who chooses the keys can break that assumption on purpose.

interview.q: What makes a hash table degrade, and why can the degradation be triggered deliberately?
interview.trap: Treating the constant time as a property of the structure. It is an expectation conditional on the keys spreading, and that condition is an assumption about input that nothing in the code states.
interview.answer:
It degrades when the keys stop spreading across the array, and that can be triggered deliberately because the spreading is an assumption about the input rather than a property of the structure.

What the structure does explains the failure. Rather than searching, the location is computed from the key — so the lookup does not get faster, it stops being a lookup, because nothing is examined and rejected along the way. That is why cost does not depend on how many entries exist.

Two keys can produce the same index, so colliding entries are kept together at a position or placed elsewhere by a deterministic rule. Either way the operation examines the entries sharing that position, which is fine while few share it.

That clause is the caveat. Constant time is an expectation resting on keys being spread; if they all land in one position the structure degenerates into a list and the operation is linear. The good case and the bad case have identical code.

So the deliberate version is straightforward: an attacker who knows or can determine the hash function submits keys chosen to collide. This was demonstrated against many widely deployed web platforms in 2011, letting a small, well-formed, ordinary-looking request consume disproportionate processing time.

The shape generalises, and that is the part worth saying: it exploits the gap between the average case, which is what the system was measured against, and the worst case, reachable by anyone who chooses the inputs. Any structure whose performance depends on typical input has the same exposure, and that assumption is usually invisible in the code.

The mitigation is a per-process random seed so collisions cannot be predicted. It does not improve the worst case, which is still linear — it makes the worst case unreachable on purpose, which is a defence against a chosen input rather than an unlucky one.

Two other costs: spare capacity must be kept, so the table resizes as it fills and a resize rehashes everything, making an occasional insertion far costlier than the average — a latency spike on a write. And iteration order follows from the hash function, so relying on it relies on something never promised.
